sections.text:
Dhul-Kifl, peace be upon him, is one of the righteous prophets of the Children of Israel. God Almighty mentioned him in the Holy Qur’an in two places, along with the patient and good prophets.

His real name was said to be “Bishr ibn Ayyub” (the son of the Prophet Ayyub, peace be upon him), and he was called “Dhul-Kifl” because he undertook a great matter and fulfilled it to the fullest extent.

The story begins when the Prophet who preceded him (it was said that he was Elisha, peace be upon him) grew old and wanted a righteous man to succeed him among his people, who would judge among them and guide them.

This Prophet gathered his people and stipulated three difficult conditions for anyone who wanted to succeed him in this great position.

The Prophet said: “Who can guarantee for me that he fasts during the day, stays awake at night, and never gets angry? Should I make him my successor?”

A young man among them stood up and said with complete confidence: “I will take care of that for you.”

The Prophet replied, then repeated his question the next day, and the same young man stood up and said: “I am.”

The Prophet finally agreed and handed over to him the reins of government and judgment among the people, hence his name “Dhu al-Kifl”, meaning the one who took care of these three difficult conditions.

Indeed, Zulkifli began to fulfill his promise; He fasted all day and prayed all night in worship of God, and in the afternoon he would take a short nap to rest and then sit down to judge among the people.

Here Iblis (Satan) intervened to try to thwart Dhul-Kifl and make him break his covenant, especially with the condition of “not getting angry.”

Satan ordered his demon soldiers to anger Dhul-Kifl, but they were unable to do so, so Satan decided to take care of the matter himself.

Satan disguised himself as a poor and oppressed old man, and came to Dhul-Kifl during his nap time (his only rest time of the day).

Satan knocked on the door forcefully, so Zulkifli stood up and opened it for him, and the lying sheikh said: “I am an oppressed man, and my people wronged me and took my rights.”

The sheikh began to talk and complain for a long time until the nap time ended, and it was time for the judicial council. Zulkifli said to him calmly: “If you go to the judicial council, come to me to return your rights to you.”

But the sheikh did not come to the council, and the next day, at nap time, he knocked on the door again and complained for a long time.

Although Dhul-Kifl was tired from staying up late and fasting, he did not get angry, and said to him: “Didn’t I tell you to come to me in the gathering?”

The sheikh replied: “If they knew that you were in the council, they would deny my right, and if you were alone, they would acknowledge it!”

On the third day, Zulkifli ordered his family not to open the door to anyone while he was resting because he was very tired.

The disguised devil came, and when he found the door closed, he entered through a small hole in the window and suddenly appeared inside the room!
Zulkifli woke up surprised and said: “Did I not order the door not to be opened? How did you get in?”

He looked at the door and found it closed as he had left it, so he knew with his wisdom and the light of his insight that this was not an ordinary human being.

Zulkifli said: “Are you the enemy of God, Satan?”

Satan admitted his defeat and said: “Yes, you made me tired and failed to make you angry or break your covenant!”

Dhul-Kifl fulfilled his promise until he died, and God praised him in the Holy Qur’an, saying: (And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl - all of them were patient).

The lesson of the story of Dhul-Kifl is the virtue of fulfilling covenants, and that forbearance and controlling anger (repressing anger) are among the greatest qualities of prophets and righteous people.
